Why does fetching data cost more than computing on it?
column2: Energy goes into charging wires, and off-chip wires are long and terminated. At 45 nm, a 32-bit DRAM read costs about 640 pJ against 3.7 pJ for an FP32 multiply (Horowitz), so a MAC fed from DRAM spends over 99% of its energy on memory.

column1: How does an energy-per-bit figure cap bandwidth?
column2: Power = 8 × bandwidth × energy per bit, so \(BW_{max} = P_{budget}/(8E_b)\). At terabytes per second every picojoule per bit is tens of watts.

column1: What is a full-swing wire's energy per random bit?
column2: \(\tfrac14CV^2\): a 0→1 transition draws \(CV^2\) from the supply and happens on a quarter of random bits.

column1: How much data must be in flight to use a memory's bandwidth?
column2: Little's law: bytes in flight = bandwidth × latency. 8 TB/s at 600 ns needs 4.8 MB, about 75,000 64-byte requests; parallelism hides latency.

column1: What is the ridge point of a roofline?
column2: Peak FLOPS divided by memory bandwidth, in FLOP/byte. Kernels with lower arithmetic intensity are memory-bound.

column1: Why is LLM decoding memory-bound?
column2: At batch 1 every weight is read once per token and used for about two FLOPs, an intensity near 1–2 FLOP/byte, far below accelerators' ridge points of hundreds.

column1: What does the KV cache cost per token?
column2: \(2 \times\) layers × KV heads × head dimension × bytes per entry. For long contexts it can exceed the weights' traffic, and batching does not amortize it.

column1: Why does batching help decode throughput but not without limit?
column2: Batching shares each weight read across sequences, but each sequence brings its own KV cache, which grows with context and fills memory capacity.

column1: What is the 'memory wall' in growth rates?
column2: Peak FLOPS have grown faster than DRAM bandwidth (Gholami et al.: about 3.0× vs 1.6× every two years), so the ridge point rises and more kernels become memory-bound.

column1: Why do lower-precision formats raise the ridge point?
column2: Each halving of precision doubles (sometimes triples) the FLOPS of the same silicon while bandwidth stays fixed. A kernel whose operands shrink too only doubles its intensity, so it keeps its place only if FLOPS merely double; operands kept wider need proportionally more reuse.

column1: Why is a modelled pJ/bit lower than a measured all-in figure?
column2: Measured power includes refresh, standby, clocking and controller activity that a per-access model omits, as with HBM2's 3.9 pJ/bit model against H200's 6.86 pJ/bit under a read-intensive microbenchmark (generation and access pattern differ too).

column1: Why has the SRAM bitcell stopped shrinking?
column2: The six-transistor cell is limited by gate and contact pitches and by variation, not lithography alone; N5 to N2 stayed near 0.021 µm² while logic kept shrinking.

column1: What is array efficiency?
column2: Macro density divided by raw bitcell density: the share of a macro that is cells rather than periphery (decoders, sense amplifiers, I/O).

column1: Why does a die with much SRAM shrink less at a new node?
column2: If logic shrinks but SRAM does not, the new area is \(s + (1 - s)/x\), so the SRAM share rises and the effective shrink falls.

column1: How do SRAM arrays survive multi-bit soft errors?
column2: A particle strike can flip several neighbouring cells, so columns are interleaved: physically adjacent cells belong to different ECC words, each of which then sees at most one error.

column1: How many sigma of margin does a large array need?
column2: For yield \(Y\) over \(N\) cells without repair, \(Q(k) \approx -\ln Y/N\): about 6σ for megabytes, growing slowly with size.

column1: What sets threshold-voltage mismatch?
column2: Pelgrom's law, \(\sigma_{V_{TH}} = A_{VT}/\sqrt{WL}\) per device (the pair coefficient is \(\sqrt{2}\) larger): smaller transistors vary more, which is why tiny cells need higher minimum voltage.

column1: What is read disturb in an SRAM cell, and how does wordline underdrive help?
column2: During a read the pass gate pulls the '0' node up; if it rises past the other inverter's threshold the cell flips. Lowering the wordline weakens the pass gate, reducing the disturb at the cost of read current.

column1: What does negative-bitline write assist do?
column2: Driving the bitline below ground strengthens the pass gate during a write so it can overpower the pull-up even under mismatch.

column1: Why do longer bitlines raise density but slow reads?
column2: Periphery per bitline is amortized over more cells, but bitline capacitance grows, so the read current takes longer to develop a sense signal.

column1: How does SRAM retention mode save power?
column2: Lowering an idle array's supply cuts leakage roughly exponentially with voltage while still holding data, as long as it stays above the retention voltage.

column1: Why do 3D-stacked SRAM dies appear in products?
column2: They add cache capacity without enlarging the logic die, sidestepping the stalled bitcell scaling, at the cost of bonding and thermal constraints.

column1: What is the read current of an SRAM cell limited by?
column2: The series pass gate and pull-down transistors discharging the bitline; their weakest instance across the array sets timing.

column1: What is the DRAM charge-sharing signal?
column2: \(\Delta V = (V_{cell} - V_{pre})C_s/(C_s + C_{BL})\): the cell's small capacitor shares charge with a much larger precharged bitline.

column1: Why do bitlines have a maximum length?
column2: Each cell adds capacitance, shrinking the signal; the sense amplifier's minimum signal sets \(C_{BL} \le C_s(V_{sig}/\Delta V_{min} - 1)\).

column1: Why is the DRAM wordline boosted above the array voltage?
column2: An NMOS access transistor can only pass up to \(V_{WL} - V_{TH}\); boosting the wordline by more than \(V_{TH}\) lets the cell charge to the full bitline voltage quickly.

column1: How does a DRAM sense amplifier work?
column2: A cross-coupled latch regenerates the small bitline difference exponentially, \(t = \tau\ln(V_f/\Delta V_0)\), and in doing so restores the cell's charge.

column1: Why is a DRAM read destructive?
column2: Charge sharing disturbs the cell; the sense amplifier must write the full value back before the wordline closes.

column1: What are row hit, miss and conflict latencies?
column2: Hit: \(t_{CL}\). Miss (bank precharged): \(t_{RCD} + t_{CL}\). Conflict (another row open): \(t_{RP} + t_{RCD} + t_{CL}\).

column1: What is refresh overhead?
column2: \(t_{RFC}/t_{REFI}\): the fraction of time the device is busy refreshing. It doubles above 85 °C, when the refresh interval halves.

column1: Why does retention get worse with temperature?
column2: Leakage through junctions and the access transistor is thermally activated; a rule of thumb is that retention halves every 10 °C.

column1: What is row hammer?
column2: Repeatedly activating one row disturbs neighbouring rows' cells until they flip; thresholds have fallen as cells shrink.

column1: What does PARA do and what is its miss probability?
column2: On each activation it refreshes a neighbour with probability \(p\); after \(N\) activations a victim escapes with \((1 - p/2)^N\).

column1: Why does a 6F² cell matter?
column2: It is the standard DRAM cell footprint in units of the minimum feature; moving to 4F² (vertical transistors) or 3D stacking is the main route to more density.

column1: Why does DDR use prefetch?
column2: The DRAM core cannot cycle as fast as the pins, so each internal access fetches several words (8n, 16n) that are serialized over the faster interface.

column1: Why does DDR5 split a DIMM into two 32-bit subchannels?
column2: Burst length 16 on a 64-bit bus would fetch 128 bytes, twice a cache line; two 32-bit subchannels keep each access at 64 bytes.

column1: What is pseudo-open-drain (POD) signalling?
column2: Termination to VDDQ, so current flows only while driving low; with LVSTL (LPDDR) termination is to ground and current flows only while high.

column1: What does data bus inversion (DBI) do?
column2: If more than half of a byte's bits would draw termination current, the byte is inverted and a DBI flag set, cutting average current.

column1: Why do DDR4 and DDR5 have bank groups?
column2: So the pin rate can rise without speeding up every bank's core: column commands to different groups issue every \(t_{CCD\_S}\), to the same group only every longer \(t_{CCD\_L}\).

column1: What is a reflection coefficient?
column2: \(\Gamma = (R - Z_0)/(R + Z_0)\); a matched termination gives zero reflection, an open end +1, a short −1.

column1: What is fly-by topology and why does it need write leveling?
column2: Address and clock pass each DRAM in turn, arriving at different times; the controller trains per-chip delays so DQS aligns with each chip's clock.

column1: What are cursors of a first-order channel?
column2: For a one-UI pulse, \(h_0 = 1 - a\) and \(h_k = (1 - a)a^k\) with \(a = e^{-UI/\tau}\); post-cursors sum to \(a\).

column1: What does decision-feedback equalization do?
column2: It subtracts the known contribution of already-decided bits (post-cursors) from the current sample, opening the eye without amplifying noise.

column1: What is PAM4's eye penalty?
column2: \(20\log_{10}(M - 1)\) = 9.5 dB for PAM4 (6 dB for PAM3) at the same swing; it pays off only if the lower symbol rate saves more loss.

column1: Why does GDDR7 use PAM3?
column2: PAM3 carries 1.5 bits per symbol with a smaller eye penalty than PAM4, raising the data rate on channels where NRZ's loss at full rate is too high.

column1: How do DDR, LPDDR and GDDR differ in priorities?
column2: DDR: capacity and modularity; LPDDR: low power and soldered packages; GDDR: high per-pin rates for graphics and accelerators.

column1: How does HBM get high bandwidth?
column2: Very wide (1,024 or 2,048 bits per stack) and moderately fast pins, over short interposer wires: \(B = WR/8\).

column1: Why do short interposer wires save energy?
column2: They are short, narrow and resistive, so reflections die out and they can run unterminated: energy is only \(\tfrac14CV^2\) per bit at low swing, instead of static termination current.

column1: What is a through-silicon via and its capacitance?
column2: A copper via through the thinned die, insulated by an oxide liner: a coaxial capacitor \(C = 2\pi\varepsilon L/\ln(b/a)\).

column1: Why does a tall HBM stack get hot at the base?
column2: Heat leaves through the top, so each layer's resistance carries all the heat from below: \(\Delta T = R_L[NP_b + P_cN(N - 1)/2]\), growing roughly as \(N^2\).

column1: Why does hybrid bonding help tall stacks?
column2: It removes the bump and underfill gap, cutting stack height and the gap's thermal resistance, which dominates a layer's.

column1: Why is stack yield critical?
column2: It is the product of every die's and bond's yield, \((y)^N\), so dies must be tested (known-good die) before stacking.

column1: Why does HBM consume more wafers per bit?
column2: Larger dies (TSV area), lower yield and stacking losses; HBM takes a much larger share of DRAM wafers than of bits.

column1: What limits HBM supply besides DRAM?
column2: Advanced packaging capacity (CoWoS interposers), whose output per wafer falls as interposers grow.

column1: Why is the HBM base die moving to a logic process?
column2: A logic-process base die gives faster, lower-power PHYs and room for custom logic, at the cost of a foundry partner.

column1: What is the stack-height budget?
column2: A fixed package height (775 µm, as reported for HBM4 in 2025) must hold base, core dies and gaps; more layers force thinner dies and thinner bonds.

column1: How do you estimate dies per wafer?
column2: \(\pi d^2/(4A) - \pi d/\sqrt{2A}\): area divided by die area minus an edge-loss term.

column1: How does stored charge shift a flash cell's threshold?
column2: Electrons on the storage node raise \(V_{TH}\) by \(-\Delta Q/C_{CG}\), about 10 mV per electron at 16 aF.

column1: Why does ISPP raise \(V_{TH}\) one step per pulse?
column2: Tunneling is so field-steep that each pulse ends at the same storage-node voltage; raising the gate by \(\Delta V_{pgm}\) adds \(C_{CG}\Delta V_{pgm}\) of charge, regardless of the cell's parameters.

column1: What is Fowler–Nordheim tunneling?
column2: Tunneling through a field-tilted triangular barrier, \(J = AE^2e^{-B/E}\), extremely steep in field.

column1: Why does QLC need much stronger ECC than TLC?
column2: Spacing falls from \(W/7\) to \(W/15\); the Gaussian tail turns that halving of margin into orders of magnitude more raw errors.

column1: Why can't NAND overwrite a page?
column2: Programming only adds electrons; erasing removes them but works on a whole block, because it biases the shared channel.

column1: What is a NAND string?
column2: Cells in series between one bitline contact and the source; reading a cell turns all others on with a pass voltage.

column1: Why are 3D NAND stacks built in decks?
column2: Etching straight round holes through hundreds of layers in one step is impractical; two or three decks keep each etch's aspect ratio manageable.

column1: How do you compare 3D NAND densities fairly?
column2: Divide Gb/mm² by layers × bits per cell: density per layer-bit reveals lateral improvements beyond layer count.

column1: What does CBA (CMOS bonded to array) do?
column2: Builds periphery CMOS on a separate wafer bonded to the array, so each gets its optimal thermal process and the die shrinks.

column1: How are retention bakes accelerated?
column2: Arrhenius: \(AF = \exp[(E_a/k)(1/T_u - 1/T_s)]\); valid only if the same mechanism dominates at both temperatures.

column1: What limits a NAND die's write throughput?
column2: Page size × planes / \(t_{PROG}\): hundreds of microseconds per program makes writes far slower than the interface.

column1: What does an FTL do?
column2: Maps logical addresses to physical pages, writes every update out of place, and runs garbage collection and wear leveling.

column1: How big is a page-mapped FTL's table?
column2: \((C/IU) \times\) entry bytes: about 1 GB per TB with 4 KiB units and 4-byte entries.

column1: What is write amplification?
column2: NAND writes per host write, \(A = 1/(1 - u)\) where \(u\) is the victim blocks' valid fraction.

column1: What is the FIFO write-amplification model?
column2: Under uniform random writes \(u = e^{-\alpha(1 - u)}\), \(\alpha = 1 + OP\): about 7.8 at 7% OP and 2.5 at 28%.

column1: Why does over-provisioning help endurance twice?
column2: It lowers write amplification and, at fixed user capacity, adds raw flash: \(TBW = TN_{PE}/A\).

column1: Why do sequential writes have write amplification near 1?
column2: Data written together is invalidated together, so victims are nearly empty.

column1: What is the ECC cliff?
column2: A t-error code's failure probability rises by many orders of magnitude as the mean error count approaches t.

column1: What bounds any hard-decision code?
column2: Shannon: code rate must not exceed \(1 - H(p)\); above that raw error rate, only soft information or more spare area helps.

column1: Why does soft-decision LDPC help, and what does it cost?
column2: Rereads at shifted references reveal unreliable bits, letting iterative decoding correct far more errors; each soft level adds read latency.

column1: How do queue depth, latency and IOPS relate?
column2: Little's law: commands in flight = IOPS × latency. Millions of IOPS need hundreds of outstanding commands.

column1: Does greedy garbage collection beat FIFO?
column2: By about a tenth for 64-page blocks under uniform random writes, but the gap nearly vanishes for the thousands of pages in a 3D NAND block; separating hot and cold data matters more.

column1: How does a codeword failure rate relate to UBER?
column2: A failed k-bit codeword holds about t + 1 errors, so \(\text{UBER} \approx (t + 1)P_{fail}/k\), hundreds of times below \(P_{fail}\) for 1 KiB codes.

column1: How do you size power-loss-protection capacitors?
column2: \(C = 2Pt_h/[\eta(V_1^2 - V_2^2)]\); charging to tens of volts stores energy as \(V^2\).

column1: How does MRAM store and read a bit?
column2: As a free layer's magnetization parallel or antiparallel to a reference layer; tunneling resistance differs by the TMR ratio.

column1: Why does the access transistor reduce MRAM's read margin?
column2: Its series resistance dilutes the resistance contrast, so the current contrast is smaller than the TMR.

column1: What thermal stability does an MRAM array need?
column2: \(\Delta \ge \ln(N t f_0)\) for at most one flip: logarithmic in array size and time, about 60 for tens of megabits over 10 years.

column1: Why does higher MRAM stability cost write energy?
column2: STT critical current is proportional to the barrier, hence to Δ; stable flash-replacement MRAM writes harder than cache-like MRAM.

column1: What is STT-MRAM read disturb?
column2: The read current lowers the barrier to about \(\Delta(1 - I/I_{c0})\), so reads must use a small fraction of the write current; this caps the read margin.

column1: How is a PCM cell RESET and SET?
column2: RESET melts it with a short pulse and quenches it amorphous (high R); SET holds it between crystallization and melting long enough to crystallize (low R).

column1: Why must PCM quench quickly?
column2: The melt must pass through the crystallization range faster than crystals can grow; thermal time constants of nanoseconds make this possible.

column1: What is PCM drift?
column2: Amorphous resistance rises as \((t/t_0)^\nu\), \(\nu \approx 0.1\); harmless for one bit per cell, crippling for multi-level cells.

column1: Why is ReRAM variable?
column2: Its filament's narrowest point is a few atoms wide, each about one conductance quantum (77.5 µS); moving one atom changes conductance by tens of percent.

column1: How does FeRAM read a bit?
column2: It drives the ferroelectric capacitor; a reversal releases \(2P_rA\) of charge, sensed as in DRAM. The read is destructive but needs no refresh.

column1: Where are emerging memories winning?
column2: As embedded NVM replacing embedded flash in MCUs and SoCs (MRAM, ReRAM, PCM at foundries), not against NAND on cost per bit.

column1: Why did 3D XPoint (Optane) fail commercially?
column2: It worked technically but could not beat DRAM and NAND on cost or open enough new uses; Micron exited in 2021 and Intel in 2022.

column1: What is compute-in-memory?
column2: Doing arithmetic where data sits: in analog crossbars, with digital adders beside SRAM, or with logic beside DRAM banks (PIM).

column1: How does a crossbar compute a matrix-vector product?
column2: Ohm's law multiplies (\(I = VG\)), Kirchhoff's current law sums on virtual-ground columns: \(I_j = \sum_iV_iG_{ij}\).

column1: How are signed weights stored in a crossbar?
column2: As conductance pairs \(G^+\), \(G^-\) in two columns; the output is the current difference and common offsets cancel.

column1: Why must crossbar columns be at a virtual ground?
column2: A resistive sense lets the column voltage rise with its current, reducing every cell's voltage in a data-dependent way.

column1: What limits analog CIM precision?
column2: Compute SNR \(= 1/\sigma^2\) for zero-mean products: device variation, not row count, sets effective bits (about 4 at 5%). It is a best case: error quoted relative to full scale costs the weights' crest factor squared.

column1: Why is the ADC the bottleneck of analog CIM?
column2: Each column's sum must be digitized at many bits; with bit-serial inputs and bit-sliced weights the conversions per MAC grow as \(b_xb_w\).

column1: Why do headline TOPS/W figures use low precision?
column2: With bit-serial inputs and bit-sliced weights, ADC-limited efficiency falls roughly as the square of bit width; 4-bit numbers look far better than 8-bit ones.

column1: How does DRAM PIM gain bandwidth?
column2: Logic at the banks uses the die's internal bandwidth, several times what its pins deliver.

column1: Why is PIM's speedup less than its bandwidth gain?
column2: Amdahl's law: only the memory-bound fraction accelerates; LPDDR5X-PIM's 8× bandwidth gave 3.01× tokens per second.

column1: What must accompany a TOPS/W figure?
column2: Precision, utilization and the measurement boundary (macro, chip, card, system), plus accuracy.

column1: What does utilization do to effective efficiency?
column2: Throughput = peak per PE × PEs × utilization; if power does not fall with utilization, efficiency falls with it.
